author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk

body.text: Full name: Birsa Munda · Born: 15 November 1875, Ulihatu village (then Ranchi district, Bengal Presidency; now Khunti district, Jharkhand) · Father: Sugana Munda · Mother: Karmi Hatu · Died: 9 June 1900, Ranchi jail (aged 24) · Known as: Dharti Aaba, “Father of the Earth” · Movement: the Ulgulan (1899–1900)
Early life and family

Birsa was born into a poor Munda family that moved from village to village in search of work as labourers and crop-sharers — from Ulihatu to Kurumbda and Bamba, where his elder brother Komta and his sisters were born. By the custom of the time he was named after the day of the week on which he was born. As a boy he grazed sheep in the Bohonda forest, learned the flute and the one-stringed tuila, and spent his evenings at the akhara, the village wrestling ground. For a time he lived at Ayubhatu, his maternal uncle's village.
Schooling and the mission years

Birsa began school at Salga, under the teacher Jaipal Nag, who saw his sharpness and recommended him to the German Mission School. To join it, Birsa converted to Christianity and took the name Birsa David, later Daud. After a few years he left the school. The years at Chaibasa (1886–1890) were formative: the Sardar agitation against the erosion of Munda land rights was in the air, and around 1890 Birsa and his family gave up mission membership and returned to their traditional tribal faith.
The land question

Under the traditional khuntkatti system, the descendants of a village's founding families held the land together. Colonial rule — and the landlords, thikadars and moneylenders who came with it — broke that system down: rents, forced dues and forest restrictions (protected forests were declared under the Indian Forest Act in 1893–94) pushed many Mundas from owners of their land to labourers on it. Birsa had seen this dispossession with his own eyes as his family moved in search of work, and it shaped everything he did next.
The Birsait faith

In 1895, at Chalkad in Tamar, Birsa renounced Christianity and began preaching: worship one God, give up the worship of bongas (spirits), and return to the community's own path. Followers — Mundas, Oraons and Kharias — flocked to Chalkad; he gained a reputation as a healer and preacher, and the new faith took his name: Birsait. His people called him Dharti Aaba. His slogan, remembered across the region to this day, was “Abua raj seter jana, maharani raj tundu jana” — “Let our rule begin; let the Queen's rule end.”
Arrest and prison, 1895–1897

The colonial administration moved quickly. Birsa was arrested on 24 August 1895 and sentenced to two years' imprisonment. After his release he spent about two years moving between villages, holding secret meetings and rebuilding the movement, while missionaries and officials pressed for his arrest again.
The Ulgulan — the Great Tumult

Around Christmas 1899, some 7,000 men and women assembled to herald the Ulgulan — the “Great Tumult” — a rising for Munda self-rule and the recovery of their land, forests and water. The rising spread across Khunti, Tamar, Basia and Ranchi. On Christmas Eve 1899, followers attacked missions at Murhu and Sarwada and tried to burn churches in Ranchi and Singhbhum districts. On 5 January 1900 two police constables were killed at Etkedih, and on 7 January the Khunti police station was attacked. The administration set a reward of Rs 500 on Birsa's head.
Dombari Buru, 9 January 1900

Thousands of Birsa's followers gathered at Dombari Buru, a hill in Khunti, armed largely with bows and arrows. Colonial troops under Commissioner A. Fobes and Deputy Commissioner H. C. Streattfield surrounded the hill and opened fire. In community memory it was a massacre: The Statesman reported around 400 killed, and the Mundas named the hill Topped Buru — “the mound of the dead”. Birsa himself escaped into the Singhbhum hills.
Capture and death

Birsa was arrested on 3 February 1900 in the Jamkopai forest in Chakradharpur and brought to Ranchi. Some 460 tribals were accused in 15 cases; 63 were convicted. Birsa died in Ranchi jail on 9 June 1900, aged 24. Colonial records attributed his death to cholera and dysentery; among his followers, suspicion of poisoning has persisted ever since.
Legacy

The movement faded after his death, but its pressure contributed to the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act of 1908, which prohibited the transfer of tribal land to non-tribals — a protection that still matters today. Birsa's portrait hangs in the Indian Parliament Museum, and the old Ranchi jail where he died is now the Birsa Munda Smriti Sangrahalaya (memorial museum), opened in 2021. Jharkhand state was formed on his birthday, 15 November 2000, and since 2021 the day is observed across India as Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas. The standard scholarly study of his life remains K. S. Singh's “Birsa Munda and His Movement”.

excerpt: Birsa Munda (1875–1900), revered as Dharti Aaba — “Father of the Earth” — led the Ulgulan, the great Munda uprising of 1899–1900, against colonial rule and the loss of tribal land. His full story: family, schooling, faith, prison, rebellion and legacy, compiled from published histories.

body.text: Full name: Rohidas Singh Nag · Born: 5 February 1934, Chandua village, Mayurbhanj district, Odisha · Died: 30 December 2012, Salbani, Mayurbhanj (aged 78) · Occupation: writer and linguist · Known for: inventing the Mundari Bani script · Revered as: Ol Guru
A schoolboy's invention, 1949

In 1949, Rohidas Singh Nag was a class III student in Mayurbhanj. Mundari was spoken all around him but had no script of its own — it was written, when written at all, in Devanagari, Bengali, Odia or Roman letters. The young student began designing letters for the sounds of his language and wrote the first Mundari Bani alphabet on the wall of his school, using clay.
Thirty-five letters, 1953

He kept working through his school years. By 1953 the set had grown to 35 characters — a complete first form of the script, its letterforms drawn, as they still suggest today, from shapes found in nature and daily life.
The 27-letter script, 1980

Nag later simplified his own creation. In 1980 a set of 27 letters was selected for use — the core alphabet taught today. That same year he presented the script to the then Chief Minister of Odisha, Shri J. B. Pattnaik, and submitted a memorandum seeking constitutional recognition for the Munda language. In 1996 he was felicitated by the Academy of Tribal Languages and Culture.
Carrying the demand to Delhi, 1999

In 1999, Nag went with others to submit a memorandum to the President of India, again appealing for constitutional recognition of the Munda language. Around him, organisations such as the Mundari Samaj Sanwar Jamda of Poda Astia, Mayurbhanj, pressed the community's wider demands: a place for Mundari in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, broadcasts on All India Radio, and a department for the language at North Odisha University.
The 2008 reform

In 2008 the Bharat Munda Samaj and the Mundari Samaj Sanwar Jamda worked with Nag himself to reform the script: letterforms that were confusing or hard to read and write were restyled, and new glyphs were added. This reformed version is the script in use today.
Into Unicode, 2022

A formal proposal to encode Mundari Bani in the Unicode Standard was prepared by Lawrence Wolf-Sonkin and Biswajit Mandal in 2021. The script was accepted and published in Unicode 15.0 in September 2022 (block U+1E4D0–U+1E4FF) — ten years after Nag's death. That is why Mundari Bani can now be typed on phones and computers, and why it appears beside every Mundari word on this website.
Legacy

Nag is remembered as Ol Guru — the teacher. A writer and poet as well as the script's creator, he spent more than six decades on a single conviction: that a community survives through its language, and a language survives through its own script. The full alphabet chart, with every letter, is on this site's Script page.

title: Mundari: language, identity and living knowledge
author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk
excerpt: An introduction to the language and the importance of documenting it with care, context and community voices.

body.text: Mundari is a language of the Munda communities, with speakers across parts of eastern and central India and beyond. Like every living language, it carries ways of describing relationships, land, work, memory and the world.
A language lives through its speakers

Language preservation is not only about recording words. It also means supporting everyday use, intergenerational learning, songs, oral histories, local expressions and the many contexts in which people communicate.
Document with care

Spelling, pronunciation and usage can vary by region and speaker. A responsible language resource should record who shared a word, where it is used, how it is pronounced and whether a native-speaker review has taken place.

title: Why oral histories matter
author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk
excerpt: Family memories and community accounts can preserve details that formal archives may not contain.

body.text: An oral history is a recorded account of a person's memories and experiences. It can help future generations understand how people remember places, livelihoods, celebrations, change and community life.
Listen before recording
Explain how a recording may be used, ask what should remain private, and allow the speaker to pause or withdraw permission. Do not assume every story is intended for public sharing.

title: Building a respectful community archive
author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk
excerpt: A practical guide to credit, consent and context when sharing photographs, documents and cultural knowledge.

body.text: A community archive can bring together photographs, documents, recordings and stories that help people explore their heritage. The value of an archive depends on how material was collected and described.
Ask permission and give credit
Before publishing a photograph, recording or document, confirm who owns it and whether the project has permission to display it. Credit the creator or contributor in the way they request.

title: Jaipal Singh Munda (1903–1970) — Marang Gomke, the Great Leader
author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk
excerpt: Jaipal Singh Munda captained India to its first Olympic hockey gold, spoke for millions of Adivasis in the Constituent Assembly — “I am proud to be a Jungli” — and founded the Jharkhand Party to demand a homeland for his people.

image.caption: The Indian hockey team at the 1928 Amsterdam Olympics, captained by Jaipal Singh Munda — India won the gold medal without conceding a single goal.
image.credit: Photo: Unknown photographer (1928) · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: Born: 3 January 1903, Takra Pahantoli village, Khunti (then in Ranchi district, Bengal Presidency; now in Jharkhand) · Died: 20 March 1970, New Delhi · Remembered as: Marang Gomke — “the Great Leader”.
A cattle-herding boy from Khunti

Jaipal Singh was born into a Christian Munda family — his father Amru Pahan and mother Radhamani — in a small village in the Khunti hills. As a boy he tended the family's cattle and studied first at the village church school, then at St Paul's School in Ranchi, run by the SPG mission. The missionaries, seeing both his sharp mind and his gift for hockey, sent him to England — a journey few Adivasi boys of his generation could even imagine.
Oxford, and an Olympic gold

At St John's College, Oxford, he read PPE and took his BA in 1926, captained the college hockey team, and became the first Indian student to be awarded an Oxford Blue in hockey. He also wrote hockey columns for the London press. In 1927–28 he was a probationer of the Indian Civil Service — and in May 1928 he captained the first Indian hockey team ever to play at an Olympic Games, at Amsterdam. India won the tournament without conceding a single goal, beating the Netherlands 3–0 in the final. Jaipal himself missed that final: as his own memoir tells it, the India Office's refusal of leave for his ICS probation forced him out, and vice-captain Broome Pinniger led the side in the last match. Afterwards he resigned from the ICS altogether.
Teacher, executive, organiser

From 1928 to 1933 he worked as a senior executive with the Burmah-Shell oil company in Calcutta, and in 1929 he founded the hockey team of the Mohun Bagan club. He then taught at the Prince of Wales College at Achimota, on the Gold Coast (today's Ghana), returned to India in 1937 as Principal of Rajkumar College, Raipur, and served the princely state of Bikaner — before turning, fully, to the cause of his own people.
“I am proud to be a Jungli”

The Adivasi Mahasabha, formed in 1938 to bring together the tribal organisations of Chota Nagpur, elected him its first president in 1939, and in that role he raised the demand for a separate Jharkhand province. Elected to the Constituent Assembly in 1946 to represent the tribal communities, he rose on 19 December 1946, during the debate on the Objectives Resolution, and spoke on behalf of more than thirty million Adivasis: “I am proud to be a Jungli” — and, in words still quoted today: “You cannot teach democracy to the tribal people; you have to learn democratic ways from them. They are the most democratic people on earth.”
The Jharkhand Party and Parliament

After independence the Mahasabha was reorganised as the Jharkhand Party (1949–50), open to non-tribals as well, with Jaipal Singh as its first president. In the first general election of 1952 he won the Ranchi (West) Lok Sabha seat with about sixty per cent of the vote, and his party won 32 seats in the Bihar assembly, becoming its principal opposition. In 1955 the party's memorandum demanding a Jharkhand state was rejected by the States Reorganisation Commission. He was re-elected in 1957 and 1962; in 1963 he merged the declining Jharkhand Party into the Congress, and in 1967 he won once more, from Khunti — sitting in the Lok Sabha continuously from 1952 until his death.
Legacy

Jaipal Singh Munda died in New Delhi on 20 March 1970, aged 67. The Adivasis of Chota Nagpur remember him as Marang Gomke, the Great Leader. The hockey stadium in Ranchi bears his name — the Marang Gomke Jaipal Singh Munda Hockey Stadium, opened in 2013 — and the Jharkhand government runs an overseas scholarship in his name for students from marginalised communities. His autobiography, Lo Bir Sendra (“A Hunter in the Burning Forest”), written in 1969, was published in 2004. Thirty years after his death, on 15 November 2000, the state of Jharkhand was finally created — the homeland he had demanded all his life.
